idiom_name: Pekko typed actor + mailbox + ask pattern
implementation_notes: An actor is a complete active object: ActorRef is the proxy, the mailbox is the activation queue, the actor's message loop is the scheduler running on the dispatcher, and the actor's state is confined to one message at a time so no locks are needed. Request/response methods use the ask pattern, which returns a Future - the pattern's Future role. Guarding, ordering and priority are expressed through the message protocol and the mailbox configuration rather than through method-request guards.
pitfalls: An actor runs one message at a time but Future continuations interleave: never mutate actor state from a callback - pipe the result back as a message.
ask creates a temporary actor per request and has a timeout; a reply that never arrives leaks references until the timeout fires.
Mailbox bounds are configuration: with the default unbounded mailbox a slow actor accumulates messages silently.

variants.name: scala.concurrent Future on a one-thread ExecutionContext
variants.implementation_notes: The standard-library route builds the pattern from scala.concurrent: the proxy returns Future[T] produced by Future { ... } (or a Promise completed by a worker), and the ExecutionContext decides where the body runs - a single-thread executor serializes the servant, replacing both activation queue and scheduler with the executor's own queue. The docs describe an ExecutionContext as an abstraction over something that can execute program logic, so passing a dedicated one is the design decision that preserves confinement; the global EC is a pool and breaks it.
pitfalls: scala.concurrent.ExecutionContext.Implicits.global is a pool: using it silently parallelizes the servant and reintroduces races.
Never Await.result inside a Future body scheduled on the same single-thread EC - self-deadlock.
Future bodies capture the servant and the EC owns a thread; shut the executor down at teardown or the JVM will not exit.
